listenings.text: Welcome back to the workshop. Before the break I promised you a simple definition, so here it is. Price elasticity is one question: if I change the price, what happens to demand? Some products are elastic. You raise the price two percent and people buy much less, because they can choose a competitor on the same shelf. Other products are not elastic at all. Bread, milk, coffee. People buy them anyway. The mistake I see most often is a company that treats every product in the same way. We have been studying this in food retail for ten years, and the answer is always the same: the number on the shelf is not the strategy. The question behind the number is the strategy.

And now the story of the week. A supermarket group in the north of England has been testing a new pricing model since January. They did not cut every price. They chose two hundred products, the ones customers remember, and they reduced those. Everything else stayed the same. The result surprised the market. Total revenue is up four percent, and the group has been gaining customers from two larger competitors every month since March. The chief executive told us the hard part was not the model. The hard part was explaining the trade-off to the board, because for three months the numbers looked worse before they looked better.

extra_audio.text: First, the team looks at the demand for one SKU. Then it forecasts what happens if the price goes up or down. After that, it measures the price elasticity of that product. Next, it compares the trade-off between volume and margin. Finally, it explains the value proposition to the commercial director.
